name: The Experience Machine
statement: Offered a machine that could give you any blissful experience you wanted for life, most people would refuse to plug in.
statementAccent: most people would refuse to plug in
meaning: The experience machine is a thought experiment devised by the philosopher Robert Nozick in his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia to argue against hedonism, the view that pleasure or pleasurable experience is the only thing that matters for a good life. Nozick asks you to imagine a machine that could give you any experiences you desired, indistinguishable from real ones: you could believe and feel you were writing a great novel, making a friend, or reading a book, all while floating in a tank with electrodes wired to your brain. Once plugged in, you would not know you were in the machine; it would seem entirely real. Nozick claims that most people would decline to plug in for life, and that this reluctance shows we value more than just how our experiences feel from the inside, that we care about actually doing things and being a certain kind of person, and about being in contact with reality.
mechanism: The argument works by testing hedonism against intuition. If only the felt quality of experience mattered, then a machine guaranteeing a lifetime of the most desirable experiences should be an offer no one could rationally refuse, since it dominates real life on the one dimension that supposedly counts. Yet Nozick argues most people would not plug in, and he offers reasons why: we want to actually do certain things, not merely have the experience of doing them; we want to be a certain sort of person, and someone floating in a tank is nothing in particular; and plugging in limits us to a man-made reality, cutting us off from any deeper or actual contact with the world. If these reasons are sound, then something besides pleasurable experience matters to us, and hedonism is false. A common objection is that the intuition may reflect status quo bias, a preference for the life one already has, rather than a real insight about value.

examples.text: A machine promises a lifetime of any experiences you choose, indistinguishable from reality; Nozick predicts most people, asked to plug in for good, would say no.
We want actually to write the novel or make the friend, not merely to have the vivid experience of doing so, which the machine could supply equally well.
Critics answer that refusing the machine may just reflect attachment to one's existing life; people asked to leave a machine they were already in might likewise refuse.

variants.name: The argument against hedonism
variants.text: Nozick's use of the machine to show that if we would not plug in, then pleasurable experience is not the only thing we value, refuting experiential hedonism.

variants.name: The status-quo-bias reply
variants.text: The objection that the reluctance to plug in reflects a bias toward the familiar rather than a genuine judgement that reality matters more than experience.

whyItMatters: The experience machine is among the most famous arguments in ethics about the nature of well-being, a standard challenge to hedonism and to any theory that equates the good life with good experiences. It gives concrete form to the thought that we care about more than how life feels from the inside, that contact with reality, genuine achievement, and being a real person are values in their own right. The experiment has shaped decades of debate over theories of well-being, from hedonism to desire-satisfaction and objective-list views, and it has gained fresh relevance in an age of immersive virtual reality and digital experience. Its influence is matched by the vigour of the replies it provokes, especially the charge that its central intuition may be an artefact of status quo bias rather than a window onto what really matters.

working.text: stipulate the machine can supply any experiences you want, indistinguishable from real ones, so pleasure is fully maximised inside the tank.
notice that most people would still decline to plug in for life, which suggests they value something beyond the quality of their experiences.
identify the goods the machine cannot give, actually doing things, being a real person, contact with reality, as candidates for what matters besides pleasure.

limits: The argument relies on the empirical and intuitive claim that most people would refuse to plug in and that their refusal tracks a genuine value rather than a bias, both of which are contested. The prominent status-quo-bias objection holds that reluctance reflects attachment to one's current life, not an insight that reality matters, and some studies of framing support this worry. The experiment tells against experiential hedonism specifically; it leaves open which positive theory of well-being is correct, whether desire-satisfaction, an objective list, or another. So it functions as a powerful counterexample to one view rather than a proof of any particular alternative, and its force depends on how much trust the guiding intuition can bear.
misreadings: The machine is an argument against hedonism about well-being, not a claim that pleasure is worthless or that virtual experience is always bad; it shows only that pleasurable experience is not the sole good. Refusing to plug in is meant to reveal that we value reality and real activity, though critics argue the refusal may instead reflect status quo bias, so the intuition is not beyond question. And the experiment does not by itself establish any positive theory of the good life; it undercuts one answer, leaving the correct account of well-being still to be settled.
origin: Introduced by the philosopher Robert Nozick in his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia as an argument against hedonism, showing that if we would decline a lifetime of guaranteed pleasurable experience, then experience is not all we value.
